opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it came from two directions at once.

The first was my own experience as a mathematician. When you write a proof on paper, a lot of the reasoning lives in the gaps: "it's easy to see," "by a standard argument," "the remaining cases are similar." Human readers fill those gaps with intuition and trust. But when I started thinking about how a machine would learn mathematics, those gaps become the whole problem. A language model can produce something that reads like a beautiful proof and still be wrong in a subtle step, and you often can't tell without a very careful expert spending hours checking it.

Lean changes that. In a formal language every step has to be justified down to the axioms, and the kernel either accepts the proof or it doesn't. So instead of relying on a human grader or a fuzzy reward, you get a perfect verifier. That matters enormously for AI, because the most powerful training paradigm we have, reinforcement learning, works best when the reward signal is clean and can't be gamed. Lean gives you exactly that: a ground truth signal for mathematical correctness.

The second direction was seeing the ecosystem mature. A few years ago formal mathematics felt like a niche hobby, very painful to write by hand. Then Mathlib grew into a huge, community-built library covering a large part of undergraduate and increasingly research-level mathematics. That meant there was a real corpus of formalized knowledge to learn from and build on, plus a community of mathematicians actually invested in it.

When you put those together, a verifier that can't be fooled and a growing body of formal mathematics, you get something very rare in AI: a domain where the system can generate its own attempts, check them with certainty, and improve from that feedback at scale. Natural-language reasoning is still essential. It's where intuition and strategy live. But I came to see Lean as the backbone that keeps everything honest. The vision is to combine the two: let the model think informally the way a mathematician does, and then ground every claim in something verifiable.

And beyond the technical reasons, there's a philosophical appeal. Mathematics is supposed to be the domain of absolute certainty. If we're going to have AI systems producing new mathematics, possibly faster than humans can read it, we need a way to trust the output without relying on reputation or authority. Formal verification is that way. So for me Lean wasn't just a convenient format. It felt like the right foundation for a future where humans and AI do mathematics together.

r001.rationale: The response motivates Lean through formal verification and mathematical certainty, but does not mention constitutional law or its comparatively precise structure as an analogy.

r002.rationale: It says Lean requires each proof step to be justified in a formal language, but does not identify translating mathematics into code as a reason Lean could support AI mathematics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, it came out of frustration more than vision at first. I spent years as a mathematician, and the thing that always nagged me was that mathematics is supposed to be the one discipline where truth is absolute, yet in practice we verify proofs socially. A paper gets refereed by two or three people who are busy, who skim, and who extend a lot of trust to the author's reputation. Errors survive for years. So I already had this sense that the way we certified mathematical knowledge was far weaker than the knowledge itself deserved.

Then I started paying attention to what large language models were doing. They were getting genuinely good at producing plausible mathematical text, but plausible is exactly the problem. A model can write a proof that reads beautifully and is wrong in one line, and if you're relying on a human to catch it, you've just made the refereeing bottleneck worse, not better. That's when it clicked for me that the issue wasn't the model's intelligence, it was the absence of a ground truth signal. In natural language there is no oracle. You can't ask "is this proof correct" and get a yes or no.

Lean gives you that oracle. When a proof compiles, it's correct, full stop, modulo the trustworthiness of a very small kernel. And that changes everything about how you can use AI. It means you can let a model try a million times and only keep what checks. It means you can do reinforcement learning with a reward that's actually honest rather than a proxy. It means a result produced by a machine can be trusted by a human who never reads it, which is the only way machine-generated mathematics can scale.

What convinced me it was Lean specifically, rather than Coq or Isabelle, was Mathlib. For the first time there was a unified, actively growing library covering a huge swath of undergraduate and increasingly research-level mathematics, built by a real community of mathematicians rather than only by logicians. That matters because a formal system is only as useful as what's already in it. If you have to build the foundations every time, nothing gets done. Mathlib meant the infrastructure was there, and the people maintaining it cared about the same mathematics I cared about.

So I came to see Lean less as a programming language and more as a shared substrate where humans and machines can meet. A human can state a conjecture precisely, a machine can search for a proof, the kernel adjudicates, and the result goes back into the library for everyone. That loop, with verification at the center, is what made me believe this was the right representation to bet on.

astra-6.text:
What appealed to me about Lean was that it gives you a way to separate generating a mathematical argument from checking whether that argument is correct. A language model can produce something that reads like a convincing proof, but there may be a gap hidden in it. In Lean, you have to make the argument precise enough for the proof checker to accept it.

And that creates a useful feedback loop for AI. You have a statement you’re trying to prove, a set of assumptions, and a precise description of what remains to be shown. The model can propose a step, get feedback, and try again. So you’re not relying only on whether the output sounds mathematically plausible.

I wouldn’t equate formal verification with mathematical creativity—choosing the right definitions or finding an interesting conjecture is a different challenge. But having a representation where you can reliably check the result seemed like a very promising foundation.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the appeal of Lean is that it gives you a precise language for mathematics and a way to check whether a proof is actually correct. With natural language, an AI can produce something that sounds convincing, but there might be a gap that’s difficult to notice. In Lean, you have to make the reasoning explicit, and the proof checker gives you feedback.

That makes it a promising environment for AI: the model can propose a step, get feedback, and try again. Of course, choosing the right definitions or finding the key idea is still hard. But having a representation where you can reliably verify the result gives you a foundation for tackling those harder problems.
